sources.note: Evaluates on-policy distillation across sampling budgets from 1 to 1024 and finds it consistently improves accuracy at small budgets while losing to the untrained base model at large ones, so what it transfers is sampling efficiency rather than capability -- and off-policy distillation, tested the same way, does expand the boundary.
sources.title: Towards Understanding On-Policy Distillation through the Lens of Test-Time Scaling

sources.note: Measures RLVR-trained models against their base models with pass@k at large k and finds the base wins, concluding RLVR sharpens sampling toward paths the base already had rather than adding new ones.
sources.title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?

result.definition: How readily a model reaches a solution it is capable of reaching, as distinct from whether it can reach it at all -- and the distinction the archive's post-training entries most often turn on. Operationally it is measured by average correctness over sampled responses, or by comparing a trained model's single-sample accuracy against its base model's accuracy at a large budget, treating the base as the upper bound. Both sources find the same separation under different training signals. Under verifiable-reward RL, six algorithms show only minor variation in the resulting gap and all remain far from the base-model bound, so what they differ in is not what they add. Under on-policy distillation from a stronger teacher, average correctness rises at every budget from 1 to 1024 while the large-budget pass rate falls below the untrained base, with a problem-level accounting finding more problems forgotten than learned and the retained set carrying the gain. The consequence for reading results is direct: a pass@1 improvement is consistent with a narrowed reachable set, and only a large-budget comparison distinguishes the two.
